objections.claim_attacked: pin-swap on two macro instances to move high-fanout pins away from the most congested channel
objections.objection: Hard macros (SRAMs, PLLs, etc.) have fixed pin locations determined by the physical layout and memory compiler; you cannot 'swap' individual pins to different die-edge locations without redesigning the macro. Rotation or mirroring is possible, but pin-swapping is a standard-cell technique, not a hard-macro technique.
objections.corrected_version: The team rotated or mirrored the two macro instances to orient their high-pin-count edges away from the worst channel, or inserted buffering repeaters to split the high-fanout net and reduce pin-access demand.

objections.claim_attacked: the result reports only WNS degradation (−12 ps) with no mention of hold timing
objections.objection: Displacing cells from six channels and rerouting nets through relaxed NDRs changes both cell-to-cell distances and buffer locations. Post-CTS placement perturbations almost always create hold violations alongside setup degradation because shorter paths lose delay margin. A real signoff review would report hold WNS/TNS, not just setup.
objections.corrected_version: WNS degraded by ~12 ps on setup and hold WNS degraded by ~8–15 ps; hold was recovered by downsizing three buffers on shortened paths during incremental optimization.

objections.claim_attacked: non-default routing rules relaxed for two mid-layer metals within the channel regions only
objections.objection: 'Relaxed' NDRs in this context must mean reduced spacing to fit more tracks, but reduced spacing increases coupling capacitance and may violate foundry signoff DRC if the rule set was not pre-qualified. The story treats this as a free congestion win without mentioning crosstalk or DRC qualification.
objections.corrected_version: Track-optimized NDRs with reduced spacing were defined for M3 and M4 in the channel regions, pre-validated against the foundry signoff DRC deck, and SI analysis confirmed that increased coupling did not degrade timing on adjacent critical paths by more than 5 ps.

objections.claim_attacked: detailed-route violations dropped from ~214,000 to 340 on the next route pass
objections.objection: A 99.8% collapse of DRCs in a single pass is atypical even when congestion is relieved. Residual systematic violations—minimum metal area, end-of-line spacing, antenna—not caused by congestion usually persist and require repair iterations.
objections.corrected_version: Detailed-route violations dropped to ~4,000–8,000 on the first pass after congestion relief, then to ~600 after one repair iteration, closing to 0 after two additional iterations with minor manual ECOs on five min-area violations.

objections.claim_attacked: no mention of clock tree impact from density screens in the six channels
objections.objection: Post-CTS channels commonly contain clock buffers and repeaters. Adding placement density screens (max 65%) in and around those channels either blocks existing CTS cells or forces their relocation, which can degrade clock skew and create new hold violations. The story ignores clock tree integrity entirely.
objections.corrected_version: The density screens were applied as soft blockages that allowed existing CTS buffers to remain while preventing new cell insertion; clock skew was re-verified and remained within 45 ps of the original spec.

missing_from_story: Whether the six channels contained post-CTS clock buffers and what the skew impact was after applying density screens.
Hold timing closure status (WNS/TNS) alongside the setup timing reported.
Signoff DRC and crosstalk validation of the relaxed NDRs before they were committed.
The specific metal layers (e.g., M3, M4) used for the NDR changes and whether they were horizontal or vertical preferred-direction layers.
Whether any power-grid vias or stripes in the channels were affected by the cell displacement and required ECO.
most_defensible_part: The rejection of floorplan rework because macro placement was frozen due to derived top-level feedthroughs and power-grid stripe locations — this is a realistic and common schedule constraint in hierarchical designs.
overall_note: The scenario structure is realistic and the floorplan-freeze reasoning is exactly what happens in production, but pin-swap is not a valid hard-macro fix and the story omits hold timing, clock skew, and NDR qualification. Correct the mechanism and add the missing closure metrics.
